overview: This atlas label covers Lao kingdoms and neighboring communities from 1650 to 1783, not one state lasting unchanged through those years. It begins during late Lan Xang and continues through the emergence of Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak. The repeated broad outline does not draw their separate jurisdictions or changing outside claims. Earlier Lan Xang history and modern Laos have distinct records; the communities here were culturally and linguistically diverse.

periods.title: Late Lan Xang
periods.summary: The atlas begins before the division into successor kingdoms. Its plural label is therefore retrospective for the early part of this interval.

periods.title: Several royal centers
periods.summary: Luang Prabang and Vientiane separated in 1707; Champasak emerged in 1713. Muang Phuan retained a partly independent position.

periods.title: Siamese dominance
periods.summary: Siamese campaigns brought the Lao kingdoms under stronger external authority. The atlas ends in 1783, while their histories continued.

items.text: Just before this map begins, the Dutch merchant Gerrit Wuijsthoff traveled up the Mekong to the court of Souligna Vongsa at Vientiane in 1641. His employer, the VOC, wanted trading opportunities. His surviving journal records a foreign visitor’s encounter with an established court and river route; it is valuable evidence, but not the voice of every local resident.

The eighteenth-century kingdoms shared connections without becoming interchangeable. A study of Qing records identifies the tributary state called Nanzhang specifically with Luang Prabang, rather than the entire former Lan Xang realm. Diplomatic names could hide big differences between a royal court, its claimed dependencies and the many communities living across the region.

The Siamese campaigns beginning in 1778 reduced the autonomy of the Lao kingdoms. Vientiane was attacked, and Siamese dominance also extended to Champasak and Luang Prabang. Tribute and outside military pressure changed relationships among rulers; they did not turn all three kingdoms into one Lao state.

Agriculture, fishing, forest collecting and crafts sustained households. Ratana’s study points to Lao legal texts mentioning farm tools, animal hire and theft of rice or fish. An eighteenth-century European compilation also listed honey, wax, cotton, fruit and rice among Lan Sang’s products. Together these sources reveal useful everyday goods, rather than an exact household menu.

Learning also happened through family relationships. In a 2008 interview used by Ratana, Kongdeuane Nettavong recalled a tradition of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century aristocratic women attending sermons and teaching what they remembered to their children. This is a later account of elite practice, not proof that every girl attended the same school or that all mothers had equal opportunities.

Luang Prabang’s documented wooden-house tradition uses raised floors, long eaves and a separate kitchen at the side. Air could circulate beneath the roof, and the space below the house served work and storage. These features suited a rainy river environment. Surviving examples have been rebuilt and changed, so their present timber should not automatically be dated to this map period.

Even bedtime helped organize space. The same architectural account describes roof beams aligned with the river and rules about where sleepers placed their heads and feet, extending to neighboring houses. A house plan could carry social and spiritual meaning as well as keep rain out. These are documented Luang Prabang traditions, not a rulebook for every community inside the outline.

Wat Xieng Thong preserves a temple complex whose origins go back to the sixteenth century, before this atlas phase. Its carved, painted and gilded architectural setting formed part of Luang Prabang’s inherited religious landscape. UNESCO distinguishes this older heritage from later colonial buildings: the town visible today contains several historical layers.

The landscape was useful as well as ceremonial. UNESCO’s description of surviving Luang Prabang includes ponds used for fish farming and vegetable growing among the houses and riverbanks. This is a later conservation record of a working townscape, not proof that every pond already existed in 1700. A patch of water could help feed a neighborhood.

A palm-leaf book began with carefully prepared leaves. Library documentation describes writing scratched with an iron-tipped stylus, darkened with soot and treated with oil. Cords held the leaves between wooden covers, and cloth protected the bundle. Making a readable book required craft skill as well as knowing the words: this was a library you could literally leaf through.

A modern inventory at Vat Si Bun Hüang found a teaching manuscript whose colophon probably dates its completion to 12 October 1662. It is catalogued as BAD-21-1-0478. The carefully qualified date comes from the scribe’s calendar information. Such discoveries preserve evidence of learning during the atlas period, although the collection also contains many much later copies.

Royal-era foundations continued after the political division. Vat Si Mungkhun in Luang Prabang was founded in 1763 or 1764 during King Sotika Kumman’s reign. Later monastic collections and buildings accumulated around this institution. Its foundation date does not date every book, library room or monk’s residence found there today.

A securely dated later writing example comes from a Luang Prabang collection: รจนาแล้วยามกองงาย, translated “the writing was finished at the time of the morning drum.” This is the scholar’s Thai-script transcription of a Lao colophon, not a facsimile of its Tham Lao letters. Manuscript BAD-21-1-0479, folio 22 verso, was completed on 2 November 1843, after this map ends. The scribe recorded the moment the work was done.

Healing knowledge survives in manuscripts too, but dating matters. A 2012 study indexed entries about toothache, fever, abdominal pain and other concerns. Only three manuscripts in that study had dates, all in the twentieth century; the others were undated. They show a later record of care and knowledge preservation, not the frequency of diseases or effectiveness of treatments in the eighteenth-century kingdoms.

ending.text: There was no shared ending in 1783. Siamese dominance had already altered the kingdoms’ autonomy; Vientiane suffered another destructive Siamese attack in 1828. Luang Prabang and other Lao communities followed different later histories. Their manuscripts, institutions and cultural practices continued through political change.
